title: How Skydiving Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain skydiving: early parachute history (Charles Broadwick aka John Murray's balloon jumps, the 1783 French observatory jump, Franz Reichelt), military static lines and rip cords, the 1950s-60s rise of recreational jumping, Domina Galbert's ram-air parachute, and the 1970s tandem jumping by Peter Chase and Gloria Maybury that opened the sport to beginners. They cover terminal velocity, freefall and canopy phases, tandem vs. solo training (AFF, IAD, USPA A license), equipment costs, reserve and AAD safety devices, freefall stunts like formation flying, tracking, skysurfing and wingsuiting, record jumps by Felix Baumgartner and Joe Kittinger, and a listener mail correction about bitters and the Floyd Collins cave temperature. Josh shares his own tandem jump at about 13,000 feet.

segments.title: Opening banter and skydiving introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter, then Josh introduces skydiving. Josh shares his tandem jump experience from about 13,000 feet, and they note the sport's improved safety record.

segments.title: Skydiving safety and early parachute history
segments.summary: They give the fatality rate of about 0.28 per 100,000 jumps in 2021 versus 0.81 in 2011 and about 11 in the 1960s. They trace early jumps from a French observatory in 1783 and Franz Reichelt's 1912 Eiffel Tower death, then Charles Broadwick (John Murray), whose balloon jumps and backpack parachute design came in the 1890s and early 1900s.

segments.title: Military parachuting and the origins of recreational skydiving
segments.summary: The military developed the rip cord and static line for combat jumps. Retired military personnel likely became early instructors. Hosts note the first skydiving center opened in 1959 in Orange, Massachusetts, and that the sport grew in the 1960s and 1970s.

segments.title: Ram air parachute and tandem jumping
segments.summary: Domina Galbert, a Canadian kite designer, developed the ram air parachute in the 1960s, allowing steering. In the 1970s Peter Chase and Gloria Maybury pioneered tandem jumping, letting beginners jump with an experienced partner after a short course.

segments.title: Pre-jump briefing and sketch transition
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the ground briefing that explains the plane, altitude, and speed, then joke about a mock first-jump scene as an ad-break stand-in.

segments.title: Jump aircraft, terminal velocity and freefall
segments.summary: Jumps are typically from prop planes such as a Beechcraft King Air at 10,000 to 14,000 feet at about 100 mph. Terminal velocity is about 120 mph for a belly-down skydiver. Air friction, not mass alone, sets the rate, and skilled divers can stop and restart freefall by changing body position.

segments.title: Canopy deployment and landing
segments.summary: Canopy opening decelerates the jumper sharply, about 2.75 g. Landing speed is around 15 to 18 mph. Tandem jumpers hit a higher terminal velocity near 200 mph and need a larger drogue and canopy.

segments.title: Toyota commercial aside and training options
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh mention a past Toyota commercial that involved a wind tunnel. They then describe training routes: the USPA A license through AFF or IAD, costs of roughly $3,500, and equipment expenses.

segments.title: Freefall stunts, tracking, skysurfing, wingsuits and canopy flying
segments.summary: They cover formation flying, free flying, skysurfing, and tracking. Speed records include the terminal velocity record of about 123 mph. Wingsuits and canopy swooping are also described.

segments.title: Space jumps and high-altitude records
segments.summary: Felix Baumgartner's 2012 jump from about 127,000 feet broke the sound barrier without a plane, with about four minutes of freefall. Alan Eustace later set a record, and Joe Kittinger did a balloon jump in the 1960s.

segments.title: Equipment: parachutes, reserves, altimeters, AAD and drogue
segments.summary: They describe parachute materials (silk, then nylon with coatings), ram-air cells, reserve parachutes with pull cords, packing requirements every 180 days, altimeters, the automatic activation device, and the pilot chute, slider and drogue.

segments.title: Freefall experience and closing thoughts
segments.summary: The hosts describe the cold, quiet freefall and the calm, warming descent under canopy. Chuck says he may try it, and they plan a listener mail segment.

segments.title: Listener mail: bitters and Floyd Collins cave temperature
segments.summary: A listener notes that many people drink bitters, citing Washington Island, Wisconsin as the largest consumer. The hosts also correct an earlier episode: the Floyd Collins cave temperature was likely not steady because ice was present.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners, invite emails to stuff podcasts at iHeartRadio dot com, and close the show.
